meta_description: 6 nights from ₹35,000 for families by private car: Kalimpong's monasteries, a night on Deolo hill, Lava's forest and a Kanchenjunga dawn at Rishyap.
summary: Six nights at a gentle pace for families, about ₹35,000 per person, twin sharing, by reserved car. Two nights in Kalimpong, one on top of Deolo hill, two in the forest at Lava and a last night at Rishyap, 2,591 m, for a Kanchenjunga sunrise. No day has more than about 35 km of driving between stays.
intro: Children remember stories, so this trip has a few. On Deolo hill, Kalimpong's highest point at 1,704 m, there is a Science Centre and paragliders to watch; at its foot are Dr Graham's Homes, started in 1900 by the Rev. Dr John Anderson Graham with just six children in a cottage. In town, Father André Butty, a Swiss Jesuit refused entry to Tibet in the 1950s, set up a dairy whose hand-rolled milk sweets are still called Kalimpong lollipops. Further east at Lava, the forest of Neora Valley National Park begins, and above it Rishyap looks out at Kanchenjunga.

We keep the days short and the nights in places with proper beds: two state-run lodges, a forest department compound and one family homestay. A reserved car with the same driver stays with you, so a tired child is never a problem. The drive up from Siliguri normally takes NH10, which has had repeated closures since October 2023; drivers then use Gajoldoba and Odlabari, the Gorubathan–Lava road (NH717A) or Darjeeling and Peshok, so check current status before you travel. Kanchenjunga shows best from October to December.
highlights: A night on top of Deolo hill, 1,704 m, at the state tourist lodge
The Science Centre on Deolo and paragliders launching overhead
A short, guided family walk inside Neora Valley National Park
Kagyu Thekchen Ling Monastery at Lava, opened in 1990
Kanchenjunga at sunrise from Tiffin Dara above Rishyap

days.title: NJP up to Kalimpong by car
days.text: Your driver meets you at NJP or Bagdogra. At Sevoke the road crosses the Coronation Bridge, built in 1937–41 and named for the coronation of George VI, a good first story for the car. The usual road then follows NH10 up the Teesta. NH10 has had repeated closures since October 2023, and on those days drivers go round by Gajoldoba and Odlabari, the Gorubathan–Lava road or Darjeeling and Peshok, which takes longer. Check current status before you travel and pack snacks. Check in at Tashiding Tourist Lodge, a colonial-era building in the Morgan House grounds on Durpin hill, and let everyone run on the lawns.

days.title: Monastery, nurseries and lollipops
days.text: Walk down Durpin to Zang Dhok Palri Phodang, established in 1957 and consecrated by the 14th Dalai Lama in 1976. Inside are the 108 volumes of the Kangyur; children can count the prayer wheels outside, turning them clockwise. Then drive to a nursery. About 300 orchid species grow around Kalimpong, and Pine View Nursery keeps a cactus collection that younger children tend to love. If it is a Wednesday or Saturday, visit the haat bazaar, confirming the day locally. Finish with Kalimpong lollipops, the milk sweets first made at Father André Butty's Swiss Welfare Dairy, which closed in 1990; others still make them today.

days.title: A night on top of Deolo hill
days.text: Drive 5–6 km to Deolo hill, 1,704 m. On the way, stop by Dr Graham's Homes at its foot. The Rev. Dr John Anderson Graham opened it in 1900 as the St Andrew's Colonial Homes for Anglo-Indian children, beginning with six children in a single cottage; it is a working school, so ask at the gate before going in. At the top, visit the Science Centre and watch the tandem paragliders take off; flights cost ₹2,500–4,500 and are for older children and adults only, depending on the operator. The Deolo Tourist Lodge sits on the hilltop, so when the day visitors leave, the hill is yours.

days.title: Over the hills to Lava
days.drive: ≈ 35 km · 1.5–2 h via Kalimpong and Algarah
days.text: After breakfast on the hill, drive back through Kalimpong and east via Algarah to Lava, about 2,195 m and 30–34 km from town. Stop at Algarah for tea and a stretch. Check in at the WBFDC Lava Eco Tourism Centre, set in a forest compound with cottages, and order dinner from the canteen. In the afternoon walk to Kagyu Thekchen Ling Monastery beside the Neora reservoir. It was founded by the 3rd Jamgon Kongtrul Rinpoche and opened on 6 June 1990. Point out to the children that the river below supplies the taps in Kalimpong: the Neora is the town's main source of water.

days.title: A family morning in Neora Valley
days.drive: Forest vehicle, set by the Lava range office
days.text: Neora Valley National Park was set up in 1986 and runs from 183 m to about 3,200 m. Red pandas, clouded leopards and Himalayan black bears live in its upper forest; with children, expect birds, giant trees and perhaps fresh tracks instead. The Lava range office issues the permit and a compulsory guide: about ₹150–300 entry each, ₹600–1,000 for the guide and a vehicle fee. Keep it to a morning. The park closes roughly mid-June to mid-September, so check current status before you travel. If it is shut, drive 8 km to Kolakham and about 4 km on to Changey Falls, a 900 m walk from the roadhead.
days.spend: ₹150–300 entry each + guide and vehicle share

days.title: Up the road to Rishyap
days.text: Rishyap sits at 2,591 m, about 10 km by road from Lava. There is a 4 km forest path too, but it climbs steeply, so with children we take the car. Sherpa and Lepcha families here began hosting guests in 1998. The local explanation of the name is ri, a peak, and shyap, old trees, which makes a good guessing game on the way up. After lunch, walk the village and scout the 1 km path to Tiffin Dara in daylight, so tomorrow's dark walk feels familiar. Dinner is early and warm. Lay out jackets, caps and a torch for each child before bed.

days.title: Tiffin Dara dawn and home
days.text: Walk the 1 km to Tiffin Dara before sunrise and wait for the first light to reach Kanchenjunga; October to December gives the best chance. Carry hot water in a flask. Back for breakfast, then drive down via Lava. Your driver will choose between the Gorubathan–Lava road, NH717A, and the road through Kalimpong to Siliguri, depending on which is open. NH10 has had repeated landslide and flood closures since October 2023, and the other ways round are Gajoldoba and Odlabari or Darjeeling and Peshok. Check current status before you travel and book an evening train or flight.

save_money: Ask each lodge about an extra bed for a child instead of a second room; it usually costs far less.
Book the Tashiding, Deolo and Lava lodges directly with the state corporations rather than through agents who add a mark-up.
Carry fruit, biscuits and a flask from Kalimpong for the Lava and Rishyap days, where shops are few.
good_to_know: NH10 has had repeated closures since October 2023; drivers use Gajoldoba and Odlabari, the Gorubathan–Lava road (NH717A) or Darjeeling and Peshok, so check current status before you travel.
Neora Valley National Park closes roughly mid-June to mid-September; permits and the compulsory guide come from the Lava range office, so check current status before you travel.
Rishyap at 2,591 m is near freezing at night from December to February; Lava sometimes sees snow.
Hill roads bend constantly; carry motion-sickness remedies for children who need them.
Mobile signal is patchy at Lava and Rishyap; keep offline maps and cash.

faqs.q: Is this Kalimpong trip suitable for young children?
faqs.a: Yes. Drives between stays are short, about 35 km at most, and three of the six nights are in state-run lodges with proper rooms. The only early start is the 1 km walk to Tiffin Dara on the last morning, which children can skip. The highest night is Rishyap at 2,591 m, which most healthy children manage well, though nights there are cold.

faqs.q: How much does this family trip cost?
faqs.a: About ₹35,000 per person, twin sharing, from NJP or Bagdogra back again, indicative for 2025–26. That covers a reserved car for seven days, three lodge nights in Kalimpong and on Deolo, three nights in Lava and Rishyap with dinner and breakfast, other meals and entry fees. Children sharing a room cost less; ask each lodge about extra beds.

faqs.q: Why stay overnight on Deolo hill?
faqs.a: Most visitors see Deolo in an hour and leave. Staying at the WBTDC Deolo Tourist Lodge on the 1,704 m hilltop lets you have the lawns and the views to yourselves in the evening and early morning, when the day crowds are gone. Children can watch the paragliders by day and the town lights by night. Rooms cost about ₹2,500–4,500 indicative.

It depends on the operator. Tandem flights from Deolo cost about ₹2,500–4,500, with a trained pilot, and operators set their own age, weight and health rules. Many families let teenagers fly and younger children watch. Flights stop in wind, rain or cloud. Ask at the launch site, check the operator's safety record, and never feel obliged to fly.

Dr Graham's Homes is a school at the foot of Deolo hill. The Scottish missionary Rev. Dr John Anderson Graham founded it in 1900 as the St Andrew's Colonial Homes for Anglo-Indian children, starting with six children in a cottage. It is still a working school, so treat visits with care: ask at the gate, keep to areas you are shown and avoid school hours.

faqs.q: Is Neora Valley National Park safe for families?
faqs.a: Yes, with a guide, which is compulsory anyway. The Lava range office issues the permit and assigns a local guide; entry is about ₹150–300 each, the guide ₹600–1,000 a day, plus a vehicle fee. With children we keep to a short morning route. Wear closed shoes and long trousers. The park closes roughly mid-June to mid-September, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where do we stay on this trip?
faqs.a: Two nights at Tashiding Tourist Lodge, a WBTDC colonial-era building in the Morgan House grounds on Durpin hill, one at the WBTDC Deolo Tourist Lodge on Deolo hill, two at the WBFDC Lava Eco Tourism Centre in a forest compound, and one in a Sherpa or Lepcha family homestay at Rishyap. Book the state lodges early for October and May.

faqs.q: Is NH10 open for the drive to Kalimpong?
faqs.a: NH10, from Sevoke up the Teesta, has had repeated landslide and flood closures since the October 2023 Teesta flood. On those days drivers use Gajoldoba and Odlabari, the Gorubathan–Lava road (NH717A) or Darjeeling and Peshok, all longer. For a family, that means more snacks and a later lunch. Ask your driver the evening before, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the best time for a family trip to Kalimpong and Lava?
faqs.a: March to May and October to November suit families best: dry roads, mild days and clear mornings, especially in autumn. May and the Puja holidays in October are busiest, so book early. December to February is cold at Lava and Rishyap but quiet. We avoid July and August, when heavy rain brings landslides and the national park is closed.
